forecasts.label: Capital financing requirement
forecasts.note: Restated at each quarterly return. The Q4 restatement comes from the annual return itself, so it lands on the outturn by construction — the interesting movement is Q1 to Q3.

forecasts.label: Interest payable
forecasts.note: The council's own full-year forecast, restated at each quarterly return.

forecasts.label: Revenue spending (net current expenditure)
forecasts.note: The full-year forecast of net current expenditure — the running cost of services — restated each quarter against the same measure at outturn.

forecasts.label: Capital expenditure
forecasts.note: Total capital spending forecast each quarter (the capital payments return) against the annual capital outturn. Capital spending not met from grants or receipts is what turns into new borrowing, so a forecast running ahead of outturn is a borrowing signal.

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter
in_year.note: Per quarter, not cumulative. The quarterly return is a lighter collection than the annual one and sums to roughly 92% of it nationally, so the two are shown apart rather than added together.

news_drafts.headline: Burnley forecasts £52k net overspend for 2026/27 at quarter 2, down from £176k at quarter 1
news_drafts.lead:
Burnley Borough Council is forecasting a net overspend of £52k on its day-to-day budget for 2026/27, according to the quarter 2 monitoring report put to its Scrutiny Committee. The quarter 1 forecast was a net overspend of £176k. The paper expects the position to break even by the end of the year.

The quarter 2 forecast includes identified salary savings, counted as a contribution to the council's annual efficiency target. The paper says forecasts remain under review.

Within that, Green Spaces and Amenities is forecasting a net overspend of £193k, compared with £175k at quarter 1. Income from cremation, burial and interment is projected to fall £150k short for the year; the paper says that deficit is "unchanged at £150k for the year", based on receipts so far and typical September to March levels. The service also reports £25k of higher fuel costs, £6k of lost rental income at the Queens Park lodge and a £12k loss from the ice cream concession.

In the capital programme, the Minor Adaptations budget stands at £120,607 and £81,389 (67%) had been spent at mid-year. The paper says: "It is currently anticipated there will be an overspend." The service is in discussions with Lancashire County Council about it.

news_drafts.headline: Burnley lifts capital spending to £31m as debt falls and treasury returns beat forecast
news_drafts.lead: Burnley Council revised its capital spending upward by £6.2m to £31m in the first quarter of 2026–27, an 82 per cent increase on the previous year, but financed most of the rise through grants and reserves rather than new borrowing. The council's underlying borrowing need, known as its capital financing requirement, fell by £2.3m to £88.1m despite the higher spending, and its external debt decreased by £234k as scheduled repayments came due. Investment returns and debt management outperformed budget by £120k in the quarter. The council forecasts capital spending will fall sharply to £13.6m next year, suggesting the present level is a peak in a frontloaded programme. Financing costs are forecast to reach 24–28 per cent of the council's net revenue stream, nearly double the 14.7 per cent recorded in 2025–26, reflecting both elevated capital investment and the impact of higher interest rates on debt service.

news_drafts.headline: Burnley received "Reasonable Assurance" audit opinion for 2025/26 but Charter Walk acquisition had comprehensive controls
news_drafts.lead: Burnley's internal audit concluded that the council has a good system of controls but minor weaknesses in design or consistency of application may put the achievement of some objectives at risk. The council received a "Reasonable Assurance" overall audit opinion for 2025/26, the second-highest rating available. However, when auditors reviewed the council's acquisition of Charter Walk shopping centre in Burnley town centre — a decision presenting wide-ranging commercial risks — they found the risks were properly identified, controlled and continue to be monitored, and members were fully briefed before the decision. Internal audit gave comprehensive assurance that controls were sound and consistently applied, with no remedial actions required. The council implemented 100 per cent of high-priority audit recommendations against its 100 per cent target, though some lower-priority recommendations have been delayed.

findings.paper_title: Item ee - App 1 (showing tracked changes) Housing Enforcement Policy
findings.headline: Unpaid work-in-default costs will be registered as financial charges on the Local Land Charges Registry and accrue compound interest
findings.detail: Costs of carrying out work in default and related charges are invoiced to the owner. Where unpaid, the Council will register the debt as a financial charge against the property, and the paper says the charge then accrues compound interest. The Council may also seek recovery from rent where the tenant receives Housing Benefit after 30 days.
findings.matters: A debt secured as a land charge that compounds until cleared is a recovery route a finance director would weigh against write-off risk and the timing of cash collection.
findings.quote: Until cleared, all outstanding debts will be registered with the Local Land Charges Registry as a financial charge. Once registered, the charge will accrue compound interest

findings.paper_title: Item ee - App 1 (showing tracked changes) Housing Enforcement Policy
findings.headline: Maximum Rent Repayment Order period rises from 12 months to 24 months for offences committed on or after 1 May 2026
findings.detail: The policy says the Council may apply for Rent Repayment Orders, under which the Tribunal may order a landlord to repay Housing Benefit or Universal Credit paid in respect of rent. It states the maximum period has changed for offences from 1 May 2026, subject to the Tribunal's determination.
findings.matters: A longer look-back window changes how much housing benefit or universal credit a council can seek to recover through RROs, which a finance officer at another council would want to compare against their own recovery position.
findings.quote: the maximum period for which an RRO may be made has increased from 12 months to 24 months

findings.paper_title: Item ee - App 1 - Housing Enforcement Policy 2026
findings.headline: Unpaid costs of work in default are registered as a financial charge with the Local Land Charges Registry and accrue compound interest until cleared
findings.detail: Where the Council carries out work in default and the invoice is unpaid, the costs are recovered from the owner. If the invoice is unpaid after 30 days, the Council will look to recover the debt from rent where the tenant receives Housing Benefit.
findings.matters: This is a receivables mechanism: the debt sits as a charge on the property with compound interest, which affects how the Council recovers enforcement costs.
findings.quote: Until cleared, all outstanding debts will be registered with the Local Land Charges Registry as a financial charge.

findings.paper_title: Item ee - App 1 - Housing Enforcement Policy 2026
findings.headline: Rent Repayment Orders can now cover up to 24 months for offences committed on or after 1 May 2026, up from 12 months
findings.detail: The policy states that the maximum RRO period has increased under the Renters' Rights Act 2025 regime. The Council may apply for RROs where appropriate, and the Tribunal may order repayment of Housing Benefit or Universal Credit paid in respect of rent.
findings.matters: A longer recovery window changes how much of the housing benefit or universal credit paid on unlicensed or non-compliant rented properties the Council can pursue from landlords.
findings.quote: Under the RRO regime applying to offences committed on or after 1 May 2026, the maximum period for which an RRO may be made has increased from 12 months to 24 months

findings.paper_title: Cap Bud Mon App 2 Capital Financing Qtr 2 2627 v3
findings.headline: Better Care Grant funds £3,378,236 of Housing & Development Control capital works, the largest single financing line in that service area.
findings.detail: The Better Care Grant row sits within the Housing & Development Control table and shows a revised budget of £3,378,236. The row has no other financing amounts, so the grant funds the full figure. The table does not show grant conditions, claim timing or any change from the original allocation.
findings.matters: A grant-funded housing programme of this size depends on continued central government funding, which a finance director at another council would compare against their own grant allocations.
